title: "Chapter 7 - High-Dimensional Applications"
description: "Connect actuator and contact assumptions to finite-time delivery and robustness without inferring a human control law."

## Start With the Mechanical Question

Human and robotic motion both involve coupled mechanics, actuator limits and imperfect observations. Neither category has a universal advantage in smoothness or robustness. A useful model states what is measured, what is commanded, what is inferred, and which errors matter to the task.

For generalized coordinates $q\in\mathbb R^d$, a mechanical model can be written

$$
\begin{aligned}
&H(q)\ddot q+C(q,\dot q)\dot q+g(q)\\
&\qquad=B_\tau(q)u_\tau+J_c(q)^\top f_c.
\end{aligned}
$$

Here $H$ is inertia, $B_\tau$ maps actuator forces, and $f_c$ denotes constraint reactions. The mechanical state is $(q,\dot q)$, of dimension $2d$ in independent coordinates, before adding actuator or estimator states. A degree of freedom is not one segment mass. Inertia and a contraction metric are different objects, generally with different dimensions and units.

## Close Actuation and Contact Before Linearizing

An ideal torque model can be input-affine. If the commanded input is excitation, activation and muscle-tendon dynamics must be specified; muscle force contains active and passive contributions. Zero excitation can leave nonzero force because internal states persist. The exact model variant decides input affinity and smoothness.

For a fixed sticking contact mode, include position, velocity and acceleration constraints and use compatible reduced coordinates or constrained perturbations. During a true flight phase there is no ground contact. Underactuation depends on the actuator map and constrained motion, not simply a count of contact points. Impacts and switches require event/reset sensitivity. Stability of a walking cycle can concern transverse or return-map errors, rather than convergence of every state at the same clock time.

## Delivery Is a Finite-Time Output

For a golf swing, define $y=h(x(T))$ using explicit outputs, units and an impact convention. A fixed-time first variation gives $\delta y=Dh\,\delta x(T)$. If impact time changes, include that event-time contribution. Propagating initial and command perturbations to this output can identify sensitivity directions in the specified model.

A terminal penalty $Dh^\top WDh$ can emphasize face orientation or velocity while ignoring other state directions. Those ignored directions are not necessarily physiologically safe, controllable, or dynamically realizable. A fitted swing trajectory does not uniquely determine muscle forces or neural feedback; competing internal histories can produce similar delivery.

Mechanical power transfer is force or torque paired with velocity. A sequence of segment speed peaks alone does not prove an energy-transfer mechanism. Use a declared system boundary, signed power, storage terms and contact work before connecting coupled motion to performance.

## Other Tasks Expose the Same Boundaries

A quadrotor model may be affine in rotor thrusts while differing from a model driven by rotor speed or voltage. A manipulator's task stiffness is not automatically a state-space contraction metric. Impedance stability also depends on inertia, damping, constraints and environment coupling. A Riccati identity does not certify arbitrary impedance gains.

Dense linear algebra often has cubic factors in state dimension, but runtime depends on horizon, input dimension, sparsity, derivative evaluation, solver and hardware. There is no universal cutoff at a particular number of degrees of freedom. Report measured timings for a specified implementation rather than inventing a physiological or computational threshold [@tassa2014control].

## Evidence Needed for the Swing Claim

Use measured kinematics and external forces to constrain the mechanical model, report parameter and measurement uncertainty, and test held-out delivery and perturbation responses. A model robustness certificate remains conditional on those model assumptions. Agreement with a trajectory, successful optimization, or lower simulated cost alone does not identify a golfer's neural objective.
